findings.title: Agent onInvoke example performs privileged operations without authorization
findings.description: The onInvoke example reads an app secret, invokes paid AI and managed services, makes a secret-authenticated request, writes through the app's service identity, and schedules work before checking the caller. The owning runtime's /agents route only verifies an app-scoped JWT; it does not require the caller to be an owner or privileged member. Consequently, any ordinary signed-in app user can invoke copied code with attacker-controlled jobId and query values, trigger provider requests, consume resources, poison runtime state, and cause service-authorized writes. The page correctly explains this authorization boundary for kind: backend handlers at lines 127-145, but incorrectly limits the warning to that kind even though agent invocation has the same admission boundary.
findings.recommendation: Require onInvoke handlers to fail closed on a missing acting user and then verify an owner, admin, or resource-specific role keyed by ctx.identity.user before reading secrets or performing any external, paid, scheduled, or service-identity operation. Add this warning and a secure authorization example directly to the Agent Entry section.

revalidation.reasoning: The `onInvoke` example performs storage writes, secret reads, paid AI and service calls, a secret-authenticated fetch, an app-identity data write, and scheduling before checking `ctx.identity.user` or any role. The same bounded-host `/agents/*` admission path used for this runtime verifies only that the JWT belongs to the app. The generated runtime wrapper calls `H.onInvoke(input, ctx)` directly and does not evaluate a function policy `auth` expression. The authorization warning later on the page is explicitly limited to the `kind: "backend"` fetch handler even though the agent entry has the same caller-admission boundary. An ordinary signed-in user can supply `jobId` and `query`, causing the example to make provider requests and write or schedule attacker-selected application state. The `ctx.bounded` operation runs through the app service identity, so downstream policy cannot reconstruct or authorize the original human caller. Caller billing and app-level spend caps limit some cost exposure, but they do not protect the secret-authenticated external call or privileged service-identity effects. The missing authorization gate therefore remains a high-impact exploitable flaw in the copied example.
